Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Despite acknowledgment from the White House a day earlier that a peace deal between Israel and the Palestinians is unlikely before a new U.S. president takes office, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Friday she is confident that ongoing efforts would produce success. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, right, and U.S.  Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice speak Thursday. "Carried to its state of conclusion, it will produce a state of Palestine," Rice, referring to negotiations in the wake of last year's U.S. summit on Israel-Palestinian peace in Annapolis, Maryland, said at a joint news conference with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, West Bank. Rice is on her eighth trip to the region since the Annapolis summit. On Thursday, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino said the Bush administration does not "think that it's likely that it (a peace agreement) would happen before the end of the year." Rice said Friday that she realizes the lack of a peace agreement in the months following the Annapolis summit had caused some concerns that talks had stalled or might fail, but "it's quite the opposite -- the Annapolis process has laid the foundation for the eventual establishment for the state of Palestine." The purpose of her current trip, Rice said, was "to advance the Annapolis process," and while she did not speculate on a timetable for the future of the process or offer specifics on peace talks, she added, "I've seen them move forward a great deal in the past year." Both Israeli and Palestinian officials have expressed doubts about achieving a peace agreement before President Bush leaves office, but until this week U.S. officials had been more optimistic in their public comments. Speaking in Israel on Thursday, Rice blamed part of the inability to secure a deal on recent political changes in Israel, which she noted is "in the midst of elections." With Abbas on Friday, she emphasized that the commitment expressed by Abbas and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert when they signed an agreement to work toward a peace deal by the end of 2008 is still strong. "I hope that the tremendous commitment (by both sides) is fully understood," Rice said. While Rice did not discuss any impact a new administration in Washington might have on the process, she said, "The United States really does understand why the Palestinian people want unity." Israel in recent months has seen political upheaval. Olmert resigned in September amid allegations of corruption. Kadima Party leader and Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni gave up efforts to form a new coalition government late last month and is seeking to hold early general elections, which could be held in February, Livni's spokesman has said. Olmert will continue to lead as Israel's interim prime minister until a successor assumes power either by forming a coalition in the current Knesset or through general elections. However, it is unclear whether he will be able to strike a deal with the Palestinians before Israel forms its new government. Last month, Rice postponed a trip to a Middle East conference because of the global crisis in financial markets.

(CNN) — One day after the White House conceded that an Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement probably would not be reached before the next U.S. president entered office, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Friday that she remained convinced the continuing diplomatic effort would ultimately succeed.

Rice said the negotiations launched after the U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace summit held last year in Annapolis, Maryland, would eventually result in the creation of a Palestinian state if pursued to completion. She made the remarks in Ramallah, in the West Bank, during a joint news conference with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas.

The visit marked Rice’s eighth journey to the region since the Annapolis meeting. She had appeared Thursday with Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni.

White House spokeswoman Dana Perino said Thursday that the Bush administration did not consider it likely that a peace accord would be completed by the end of the year.

Rice acknowledged Friday that the absence of an agreement in the months after Annapolis had prompted fears that the negotiations were deadlocked or destined to collapse. She argued, however, that the reverse was true, saying the Annapolis initiative had established the groundwork for the eventual creation of a Palestinian state.

She described the goal of her latest visit as moving the Annapolis effort ahead. Although she offered no details about the negotiations and declined to predict when the process might be completed, Rice said she had witnessed substantial progress during the previous year.

Israeli and Palestinian leaders had already voiced skepticism about concluding an agreement before President Bush left office. Until that week, however, U.S. officials had generally sounded more hopeful in public.

During remarks in Israel on Thursday, Rice said recent political developments there were partly responsible for the failure to finalize a deal, pointing out that the country was entering an election period.

Standing with Abbas on Friday, she stressed that both he and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert remained deeply committed to the pledge they made to pursue a peace agreement by the end of 2008. Rice said she hoped the strength of that commitment on both sides was fully recognized.

She did not address how a change of administration in Washington could affect the negotiations, but said the United States understood the Palestinian people’s desire for unity.

Israel had experienced significant political turmoil in recent months. Olmert stepped down in September while facing corruption allegations. Near the end of the following month, Livni—Israel’s foreign minister and leader of the Kadima Party—abandoned attempts to assemble a new governing coalition and began seeking early nationwide elections. Her spokesman said those elections could take place in February.

Olmert was set to remain interim prime minister until a successor took office, either by building a coalition in the existing Knesset or following a general election. It remained uncertain whether he could reach an agreement with the Palestinians before a new Israeli government was established.

The previous month, Rice had canceled a planned trip to a Middle East conference because of the worldwide financial-market crisis.

counterfactuals.output:
# Rice voices confidence in Mideast peace process despite deadline doubts

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice expressed confidence in the U.S.-backed Annapolis peace process, even as doubts grew that Israel and the Palestinians could reach a comprehensive agreement before President George W. Bush leaves office.

Rice said negotiations between Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas had established a serious framework for addressing the conflict’s most difficult issues. She acknowledged, however, that the timetable remained ambitious and that any agreement would require difficult political decisions from both sides.

The talks were launched at a November 2007 conference in Annapolis, Maryland, where Israeli and Palestinian leaders committed themselves to pursuing a peace deal by the end of 2008. The negotiations were intended to address final-status questions including Jerusalem, borders, Israeli settlements, Palestinian refugees and security.

Progress has been clouded by continued violence, Israeli settlement activity and deep divisions among Palestinians. Abbas’ authority is limited largely to the West Bank, while Hamas remains in control of the Gaza Strip.

Skepticism has also increased because the Bush administration has only a limited time left to broker an accord. Bush is scheduled to leave office in January 2009, and neither side has indicated that major breakthroughs are imminent.

Rice nevertheless argued that the process had value even if negotiators failed to complete a final agreement on schedule. Regular meetings between Israeli and Palestinian leaders, she said, had created momentum that could continue beyond the current U.S. administration.

The secretary of state has made repeated trips to the region in an effort to keep the negotiations moving and to press both sides to meet commitments under the internationally backed “road map” for peace.

U.S. officials have maintained that Washington cannot impose a settlement, but can help narrow differences and encourage the parties to make the compromises necessary for a two-state solution.

Rice’s comments reflected the administration’s determination to preserve the Annapolis initiative as a central part of Bush’s foreign-policy legacy, while leaving open the possibility that the search for an agreement could extend into the next presidency.

**BREAKING NEWS — Friday, Nov. 7, 2008**

### Rice says peace negotiations will ultimately produce Palestinian state

**RAMALLAH, West Bank** — U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Friday that ongoing Israeli-Palestinian negotiations would eventually lead to the creation of a Palestinian state, despite dimming prospects for an agreement before President George W. Bush leaves office.

Speaking after talks with Palestinian leaders, Rice said the negotiations launched at last year’s Annapolis peace conference had established a foundation for an eventual settlement. Israeli and Palestinian officials have acknowledged that they are unlikely to meet the administration’s goal of reaching an agreement by the end of 2008.

The diplomatic push has been complicated by political turmoil in Israel. Prime Minister Ehud Olmert is serving in a caretaker role after announcing plans to resign amid corruption allegations, while Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni failed to assemble a new governing coalition.

Israel is now preparing for early parliamentary elections, expected in February, raising uncertainty over whether the next government will continue the negotiations on their current terms.

Major disputes remain unresolved, including the borders of a future Palestinian state, the status of Jerusalem, Israeli settlements and the fate of Palestinian refugees. Rice nevertheless insisted that the negotiating process would endure beyond the current U.S. and Israeli administrations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed news report explaining the contrast between the White House’s pessimism about a 2008 Middle East peace deal and Condoleezza Rice’s continued optimism.
counterfactuals.output:
**White House Doubts 2008 Middle East Peace Deal as Rice Maintains Hope**

**WASHINGTON —** The White House has publicly lowered expectations that Israel and the Palestinians will reach a comprehensive peace agreement before President George W. Bush leaves office, exposing a notable contrast with Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice’s continued insistence that intensive diplomacy can still produce meaningful progress.

The administration began the year hoping that negotiations launched at the November 2007 Annapolis conference would lead to an agreement by the end of 2008. But with only weeks remaining, White House officials acknowledged that the deadline was unlikely to be met.

The change in tone reflected the widening gap between the ambitious timetable established at Annapolis and the political and security conditions confronting the two sides. Negotiators remained divided over the most difficult issues: the borders of a future Palestinian state, the status of Jerusalem, Israeli settlements, Palestinian refugees and security arrangements.

Rice, however, continued to resist declaring the process a failure. During repeated trips to Israel and the Palestinian territories, she argued that the talks had become more serious and detailed than was publicly apparent. Even if a final treaty could not be signed during the Bush administration, she suggested, the negotiations could establish a framework that the next U.S. president could carry forward.

“We continue to believe that the Annapolis process is the best way forward,” Rice said in substance during her late-stage diplomatic efforts, emphasizing that both sides remained committed to negotiations and to the goal of two states living side by side in peace and security.

### A more pessimistic White House

The White House’s assessment was more direct. Officials said privately and publicly that a complete agreement before the end of the year had become improbable. Their comments represented a retreat from Bush’s earlier confidence that the parties could conclude an accord during his presidency.

The administration did not abandon the two-state objective, but it increasingly portrayed Annapolis as the beginning of a longer process rather than a deadline-driven effort likely to culminate in 2008.

That pessimism was based partly on political instability on both sides.

Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, weakened by corruption investigations, announced that he would step down after his party selected a new leader. His reduced authority made it difficult for him to offer politically explosive concessions on Jerusalem, borders or settlements. Israel’s approach to elections also raised the possibility that a future government might take a harder line.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas faced his own legitimacy and security problems. His Fatah-led government controlled the West Bank, but Hamas remained in power in the Gaza Strip after violently ousting Abbas’s forces there in 2007. The split left Abbas unable to guarantee that any agreement would be accepted or implemented throughout the Palestinian territories.

Continued rocket fire from Gaza, Israeli military operations, settlement construction and restrictions on Palestinian movement further eroded trust.

### Rice’s case for optimism

Rice’s more hopeful position rested less on the likelihood of a formal signing ceremony than on the diplomatic structure created since Annapolis.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiating teams had held regular, largely confidential discussions. Rice argued that the secrecy surrounding those talks should not be mistaken for a lack of activity. Public disclosure of proposed compromises, she warned, could expose leaders to domestic opposition before a complete package was ready.

Her diplomacy therefore focused on preserving the negotiations, narrowing differences and documenting areas of progress. Rice also sought to ensure that neither side took unilateral steps that would prejudice a final settlement.

She continued to press Israel over settlement activity, which the United States regarded as inconsistent with obligations under the internationally backed “road map” for peace. At the same time, she called on the Palestinian Authority to strengthen its security institutions and prevent attacks against Israel.

Rice also portrayed the process as broader than a single deadline. In her view, regular negotiations, improved Palestinian security forces and greater Arab engagement could leave the next American administration with a stronger foundation than the Bush administration had inherited.

### Different messages, not necessarily different policy

The contrast between Rice and the White House was partly one of emphasis.

White House officials were assessing whether the administration’s stated objective—a completed agreement in 2008—would be achieved. On that narrow question, their answer had become increasingly pessimistic.

Rice was focusing on whether the negotiating process still had value and whether significant progress remained possible. Her optimism did not necessarily mean she expected every final-status issue to be resolved before Bush left office. Instead, she appeared determined to prevent the missed deadline from discrediting Annapolis or ending direct talks.

The distinction allowed the administration to acknowledge political reality without formally abandoning its peace initiative. The White House could concede that a treaty was unlikely, while Rice continued trying to secure understandings that might survive the presidential transition.

### A legacy at stake

The disagreement in tone also reflected the importance of Middle East diplomacy to Bush’s foreign-policy legacy. His administration had been criticized for becoming deeply engaged in Israeli-Palestinian peacemaking only in its final years, after focusing heavily on Iraq, terrorism and regional security.

A signed accord would have given Bush a major diplomatic achievement. Failure to meet the 2008 target risked reinforcing the view that the Annapolis timetable had been overly ambitious.

Rice’s persistent engagement appeared designed to produce a more modest but still defensible outcome: sustained negotiations, clearer parameters for a future agreement and a commitment by both sides not to abandon the two-state framework.

As the administration neared its end, the central question was no longer simply whether Israel and the Palestinians could sign a historic treaty in 2008. It was whether Rice could preserve enough momentum to keep the peace process alive after the White House deadline had passed.

counterfactuals.output:
## Status of Israeli–Palestinian peace talks after Annapolis

The November 2007 Annapolis summit restarted direct negotiations between Israel and the Palestinian Authority, with President George W. Bush initially hoping for an agreement before leaving office in January 2009. By late 2008, however, both sides acknowledged that the deadline would not be met. Talks had continued, often privately, but major differences remained over borders, Jerusalem, Palestinian refugees, Israeli settlements and security.

### Condoleezza Rice

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice conceded that a comprehensive agreement was unlikely before the end of 2008. She nevertheless argued that Annapolis had not failed: it had established sustained negotiations, clarified the issues and created a process that could be inherited by the next U.S. administration.

Following meetings with the parties and the Quartet at Sharm el-Sheikh in November 2008, Rice said Israeli and Palestinian negotiators regarded their discussions as “substantive and promising.” She emphasized that they had agreed to preserve confidentiality, avoid partial public disclosures and continue negotiations without interruption despite political changes in Israel and the United States.

### Mahmoud Abbas

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas likewise said that no final agreement had been reached and that important gaps persisted. He maintained that peace remained the Palestinians’ strategic choice and said negotiations should continue with whatever Israeli government emerged from the political crisis.

Abbas insisted, however, that an agreement could not avoid the core final-status issues—particularly East Jerusalem, borders, refugees, settlements and the creation of a viable Palestinian state. Palestinian officials also complained that continued Israeli settlement construction and military activity were undermining confidence in the process.

### White House response: Dana Perino

White House press secretary Dana Perino said the Bush administration remained committed to helping the parties and did not regard the approaching Israeli election as a reason to abandon negotiations. The administration recognized that its original timetable was slipping, but argued that the negotiating framework and progress already made could carry over into the next U.S. and Israeli governments.

Perino’s comments reflected Washington’s effort to distinguish between missing the 2008 deadline and the collapse of the Annapolis process itself.

### Israeli assessments

Israeli officials also acknowledged that a full agreement was unlikely by the target date. Negotiators said meaningful work had been done, but the differences were too large—and Israel’s political situation too uncertain—to conclude a comprehensive treaty.

Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, in his final months in office, suggested that peace would require far-reaching Israeli territorial withdrawals and a compromise regarding Jerusalem. Palestinian officials said Olmert had presented significant ideas, but no mutually accepted document was completed. Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, Israel’s chief negotiator, favored continued talks but opposed rushing into a vague or incomplete agreement merely to satisfy a deadline.

### Olmert’s resignation and Livni’s election push

Olmert announced in July 2008 that he would not seek reelection as leader of Kadima amid corruption investigations. After Livni won the Kadima leadership contest in September, Olmert formally submitted his resignation but remained caretaker prime minister while attempts were made to form a new government.

Livni was unable to assemble a governing coalition, chiefly because of disagreements with potential partners over budgets, religious issues and negotiations concerning Jerusalem. On October 26, 2008, she recommended early elections rather than accept what she described as excessive political demands. Elections were consequently set for February 2009.

The transition left Olmert with limited authority and made it politically difficult for Israel to undertake the concessions required for a final-status agreement. Livni said negotiations should continue, but the election campaign—and the possibility of a more conservative government—made an immediate breakthrough even less likely.

### Overall assessment

By the end of the Bush administration, Annapolis had produced regular high-level negotiations and a clearer understanding of the parties’ positions, but not a peace treaty or an agreed framework on all final-status questions. Rice, Abbas, Perino and Israeli officials generally agreed that the talks should be preserved, while also recognizing that the 2008 deadline was unattainable. Olmert’s resignation and Livni’s unsuccessful coalition effort shifted the process into a holding pattern pending Israeli elections and the arrival of a new U.S. administration.
